title: Oregon State Bar Formal Opinion No. 2025-205: Artificial Intelligence
author: Oregon State Bar Board of Governors · Legal Ethics Committee

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI supervision: Retained responsibility is not strict liability
st.an: The Oregon opinion accepts that existing managerial and supervisory duties continue to govern AI use and materially develops the cluster’s proactive-governance component by requiring clear permissible-use policies, reasonable compliance efforts, and training tailored to the specific tools, risks, and data-handling practices involved. It does not address or contradict the distinction between retained responsibility and strict liability.
qs: Managerial lawyers must establish clear policies regarding the law firm’s permissi- ble use of AI, including specifically GAI, and supervisory lawyers must make reasonable efforts to ensure that the firm’s lawyers and nonlawyers comply with their professional obligations when using such technologies.

Training must include the basics of the actual type of AI being used (rather than just AI in general), the capabilities and limitations of the tools, ethical issues in the use of that specific AI, and best practices for secure data handling, privacy, and confidentiality.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The opinion accepts qualified AI use while materially grounding the cluster’s emphasis on user capability and continuous oversight in Oregon RPC 1.1. It adds that lawyers must take reasonable steps to become competent with the specific AI they use and treat that competence as ongoing, though it does not address productivity evidence, verification burdens, apprenticeship, or labour-market effects.
qs: Discussion:                                        Competence      Oregon RPC 1.1 requires lawyers to be competent in both the law and in the tools that they use to provide legal services to clients.1 Lawyers may utilize AI in their legal practice only if they have taken reasonable steps to become competent in the use of such technology.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment model and materially develops its governance implications. It translates verification and context-specific oversight into concrete Oregon professional duties, including tool-specific training, firm policies, confidentiality safeguards, vendor due diligence, court-rule compliance and accurate billing.
qs: Training must include the basics of the actual type of AI being used (rather than just AI in general), the capabilities and limitations of the tools, ethical issues in the use of that specific AI, and best practices for secure data handling, privacy, and confidentiality.
Candor Toward the Tribunal, Truthfulness in Statements to Others, and Misconduct      Lawyers must verify any work done by or with the assistance of any third-party technology, including AI.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that AI may assist legal work but lawyers retain responsibility for verifying facts, authorities, quotations and conclusions. It also supports the cluster’s account that candour and correction matter after an error is discovered, while preserving client confidentiality. Its reported hallucination statistic illustrates risk but does not establish a universal legal-AI error rate.
qs: Lawyers who discover that they inadvertently provided the court with a false statement of fact or law must notify the court and correct the false statement without violating client confidences.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The Oregon ethics opinion directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that lawyers remain accountable for AI-assisted work. It requires accuracy review of AI-generated facts, authorities, quotations and conclusions, and requires correction after a false statement is discovered. Its cited model research underscores hallucination risk but does not itself establish a universal legal-AI error rate.
qs: Lawyers who discover that they inadvertently provided the court with a false statement of fact or law must notify the court and correct the false statement without violating client confidences.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The Oregon opinion directly supports the cluster’s central claim that legal AI remains a copilot whose practical use depends on human verification and accountability. It requires lawyers to review case-specific facts, citations, quotations and conclusions for both hallucinations and other errors, and to correct false statements made to courts. Its cited hallucination figure is appropriately limited to specified general-purpose models and court-ruling questions rather than treated as universal.
qs: Lawyers who discover that they inadvertently provided the court with a false statement of fact or law must notify the court and correct the false statement without violating client confidences.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The Oregon opinion directly supports the cluster’s supervised-AI framework. It permits AI use only with ongoing tool-specific competence, human verification, confidentiality safeguards, contextual disclosure, supervision and honest billing. It reinforces human accountability but does not itself establish that verification consumes most efficiency gains.
qs: Here, competence requires understanding the benefits and risks associated with the specific use and type of AI being used.
Candor Toward the Tribunal, Truthfulness in Statements to Others, and Misconduct      Lawyers must verify any work done by or with the assistance of any third-party technology, including AI.

st.t: Supervisory accountability: Verification must test substantive support
st.an: The Oregon opinion directly supports the cluster’s core proposition that lawyers retain responsibility for AI-assisted work and must verify substantive accuracy, including facts, citations, quotations and legal conclusions—not merely screen for fictitious authorities. It also requires correction of false statements made to courts. It does not materially develop the cluster’s supervisory-accountability or proportionate-review dimensions.
qs: Lawyers who discover that they inadvertently provided the court with a false statement of fact or law must notify the court and correct the false statement without violating client confidences.

kp.k: AI use requires continuing, tool-specific competence
kp.d: The opinion, approved in February 2025, permits Oregon lawyers to use both AI and generative AI subject to ethical conditions. Under Oregon RPC 1.1, lawyers must understand the benefits and risks of their specific tools and uses, continually reassess evolving technology, conduct vendor due diligence, and obtain research, training or professional assistance where needed. These are professional obligations rather than predictions about adoption.
qs: Lawyers may utilize AI in their legal practice only if they have taken reasonable steps to become competent in the use of such technology.
Here, competence requires understanding the benefits and risks associated with the specific use and type of AI being used.
Competence is an ongoing obligation.
Lawyers must conduct due diligence on AI and potential vendors to determine whether the product can be implemented and utilized in a manner consistent with the lawyers’ ethical duties.

kp.k: Client disclosure depends on context and material impact
kp.d: The opinion distinguishes ordinarily implied authorization for word processing and research databases from new technologies materially departing from client expectations. Disclosure is context-dependent under Oregon RPC 1.4(b) and 1.2(a), considering the matter, technological novelty, data and accuracy risks, client sophistication and instructions, reliance on AI, safeguards, and effects on fees or passed-through costs. It does not impose universal disclosure of every AI use.
qs: Lawyers may be required to disclose the use of AI to their clients under certain circumstances.
The use of word processing applications and research databases are generally considered to be impliedly authorized.
However, the use of new technologies that deviate materially from the client’s expectations concerning the scope of representation may have an impact and should be communicated to the client.

kp.k: AI time savings cannot justify inflated hourly billing
kp.d: Lawyers may charge reasonable time for case-specific research and drafting with AI, but cannot duplicate charges or falsely inflate billable hours when AI saves time. General development of AI competence is not chargeable, except learning specialized AI at a client's request under a clear agreement. The opinion applies Oregon's prohibition on illegal or clearly excessive fees and expenses rather than prescribing a new pricing model.
qs: Lawyers may charge clients for reasonable time spent for case-specific research and drafting when using AI.
To the extent the use of AI results in significant time savings, lawyers may not ethically engage in any billing practices that duplicate charges or that falsely inflate billable hours.
Otherwise, lawyers may not charge for the time spent developing competence in the use of such tools.

kp.k: AI costs require disclosure and matter-specific attribution
kp.d: Clients must be informed, preferably in writing, when actual AI costs will be passed through. Lawyers cannot duplicate overhead charges or charge clients for general research intended for their own knowledge. Where actual costs attributable to a particular matter cannot be determined, periodic specialized AI charges must remain overhead rather than being prorated among clients.
qs: Lawyers must inform their clients, preferably in writing, if they intend to charge clients for the actual costs of using AI.

Lawyers who are unable to determine the actual cost associated with a particular client’s matter may not ethically prorate the periodic charges of a specialized AI, including GAI, and instead must account for those charges as overhead.

kp.k: Open-model confidentiality risks require informed consent and safeguards
kp.d: The opinion describes open models as learning from inputs and potentially incorporating or disclosing client information. Using client information in such a model requires informed consent explaining material risks, benefits and alternatives, including possible loss of confidentiality or intellectual property rights. Without consent, sensitive information must be completely and effectively anonymized or redacted; even then, consent may remain necessary if the circumstances can reveal client identity.
qs: An open model poses confidentiality risks as it may inadvertently incorporate and disclose sensitive client data that is input by lawyers or their assistants.
If lawyers would like to use their clients’ information in an open model, lawyers must obtain their clients’ informed consent.
Lawyers must ensure that the anonymization or redaction is complete and effective, and even so, the client’s informed consent may still be required.

kp.k: Closed models still require contractual confidentiality protections
kp.d: Although the opinion considers closed models inherently more protective of confidentiality, it does not treat that designation as sufficient. Lawyers must examine provider terms and require protections governing data handling, encryption, storage, destruction, privacy and external use. They must consider consent for either model type and may also need to redact sensitive information in closed systems.
qs: The use of AI in a closed model should inherently provide greater confidentiality protection than the use of AI in an open model.
However, the mere engagement of a closed model does not absolve the necessity for a lawyer to be vigilant.
Lawyers must ensure that these contracts include provisions that address how data is to be handled, encrypted, stored, and ultimately destroyed.
If the lawyer chooses to use either a closed or open AI model, the lawyer must consider whether their clients’ consent is required.

kp.k: Firm management must govern and train AI users
kp.d: Under Oregon RPC 5.1 and 5.3, managerial lawyers must establish permissible-use policies, while supervisors must make reasonable efforts to ensure compliant AI use by lawyers and nonlawyers. Training must address the actual tools used, their capabilities and limitations, ethical issues, secure data handling and differences between open and closed models. Subordinate lawyers retain independent professional obligations under Oregon RPC 5.2.
qs: Training must include the basics of the actual type of AI being used (rather than just AI in general), the capabilities and limitations of the tools, ethical issues in the use of that specific AI, and best practices for secure data handling, privacy, and confidentiality.

Ultimately, Oregon lawyers are professionally responsible to supervise the accuracy of all their work product, including that which is produced by AI and the ethical use of AI by subordinate lawyers and nonlawyers.

kp.k: Outsourced AI use extends lawyers’ supervisory responsibilities
kp.d: The opinion extends existing outsourcing principles to external assistance that uses or may use AI. Relevant diligence includes provider competence, confidentiality, references and credentials, security protocols, hiring practices, confidentiality agreements, conflict screening and access to a legal forum for contractual violations. Outsourcing does not remove lawyers' responsibility for ethical legal representation.
qs: Lawyers have additional supervisory obligations when they rely on others outside the law firm who employ, or may employ, AI in connection with the legal representation.

Earlier opinions recognize that when outsourcing legal and nonlegal services to third-party providers, lawyers must ensure, for example, that the third party performs competently and protects the confidentiality of information relating to the representation.

kp.k: Human verification and court-rule compliance remain mandatory
kp.d: Lawyers must verify AI-assisted work, including case-specific facts, citations, quotations and conclusions, to address hallucinations and other errors. The opinion connects these duties to Oregon RPC 3.3 and 4.1, requires checking court prohibitions or disclosure requirements, and directs lawyers to correct inadvertently supplied false statements to courts without violating client confidences.
qs: Lawyers must verify any work done by or with the assistance of any third-party technology, including AI.

Lawyers must check for any rules, orders, or other requirements that the court may have in place either prohibiting the use of technology (including AI) in court filings or requiring the disclosure of its use.
Lawyers who discover that they inadvertently provided the court with a false statement of fact or law must notify the court and correct the false statement without violating client confidences.

kp.k: Reported hallucination evidence supports the opinion’s accuracy concerns
kp.d: The opinion cites Mata v. Avianca as a sanctions incident and separately reports Stanford research through a January 12, 2024 Bloomberg Law article. The reported test involved more than 200,000 legal questions and found general-purpose models hallucinated at least 75% of the time on questions about courts' core rulings. This is externally reported evidence about that task and model category, not an Oregon Bar study or a measured error rate for all legal AI tools.
qs: For example, in a test      examining more than 200,000 legal questions, AI researchers at Stanford University found      that general-purpose large language models—including Meta, Google, and OpenAI      programs—hallucinate at least 75% of the time when answering questions about a court’s      core rulings.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Oregon State Bar’s opinion permits AI-assisted legal practice subject to continuing professional responsibility, rather than predicting autonomous legal services or market displacement.
pts.d: The Board-approved opinion describes AI as already widely available and integrated into lawyers’ everyday tools, with generative AI capable of producing full legal documents. It states that adoption requires tool-specific competence, vendor due diligence, confidentiality safeguards, appropriate client communication, staff training, supervision, and human verification. Some systems can generate fabricated legal information or expose client data. The opinion treats systems it describes as closed models as offering greater confidentiality protection, but not as eliminating lawyers’ obligations to examine contracts, safeguards, and consent requirements. AI may produce significant time savings, but lawyers cannot bill fictitious hours or duplicate charges. Reasonable case-specific research and drafting time remains billable; general AI training generally does not. Actual AI costs may be passed on with client notification, but periodic charges must be overhead when costs attributable to a particular matter cannot be determined. These are current ethical interpretations and conditional operational claims, not quantified forecasts of productivity, employment, or market change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The opinion principally relies on professional-conduct rules and ethics authorities, supplemented by a sanctions case and a reported study of general-purpose models.
pts.d: The Oregon State Bar grounds its conclusions in Oregon RPC provisions concerning competence, communication, fees, confidentiality, supervision, candor, and truthfulness. It also cites ABA ethics opinions, earlier Oregon opinions, other states’ ethics guidance, and fee-related cases. These are authoritative and interpretive grounds for professional obligations, rather than empirical evidence of economic effects. For fabricated legal information, it cites Mata v. Avianca as a sanctions incident and a January 12, 2024 Bloomberg Law report describing Stanford researchers’ testing of more than 200,000 legal questions. The opinion reports that general-purpose models hallucinated at least 75% of the time on questions about courts’ core rulings; this is not presented as a measured error rate for all legal AI tools. The document provides no original empirical study or quantified evidence of AI-related time savings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The February 2025 opinion addresses present use under evolving, tool-specific and matter-specific conditions, with no forecast horizon.
pts.d: Competence is continuing because tools and their risks change rapidly. Disclosure to clients is not universally required: the opinion calls for case-by-case consideration of client expectations, technology novelty, data and accuracy risks, reliance, safeguards, instructions, and fee effects. It distinguishes ordinary impliedly authorized technology use from material deviations from client expectations. Under the opinion’s open-model description, use of client information requires informed consent; anonymization or redaction must be complete and effective and may not remove the need for consent. Closed models still require scrutiny of contractual confidentiality protections and consideration of consent. Training time for specialized AI may be billed at the client’s request under a clear agreement, but otherwise developing competence is not chargeable. Lawyers must also comply with applicable court restrictions or disclosure requirements.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The obligations affect Oregon practitioners, firm managers and supervisors, subordinate lawyers, nonlawyer assistants, outside service providers, clients, and recipients of legal work.
pts.d: Practicing lawyers retain responsibility for competence, confidentiality, billing, and the accuracy of AI-assisted work. Managerial lawyers must establish firm AI-use policies, while supervisors must ensure appropriate compliance and tool-specific training for lawyers and nonlawyers. Subordinate lawyers retain their own professional obligations despite supervisory instructions. Lawyers using outside providers must extend their diligence and supervision to those providers’ potential AI use. Clients face potential data exposure, inaccurate work, changed methods of representation, and AI-related charges; the opinion specifies communication, consent, security, and billing safeguards. Courts and third persons are affected by the risk of false statements and fabricated authorities. The opinion does not distinguish market effects by firm size or predict job losses, new staffing structures, or access-to-justice outcomes.
